name: Xylitol (birch sugar)
summary: A sweetener in gum, candy, peanut butter, and baked goods. In dogs it can cause a rapid, dangerous blood-sugar crash and liver injury. Its effect in cats is not well established.
clinical_signs: weakness; wobbliness; vomiting; collapse; seizures
common_sources: Sugar-free gum and candy, some peanut butters, baked goods, dental products.
dose_warning: Even a small amount can affect a dog.

name: Chocolate / cocoa
summary: Contains theobromine and caffeine. Darker and baking chocolate carry the most risk; large amounts can be an emergency.
clinical_signs: vomiting; restlessness; racing heart; tremors; seizures
common_sources: Candy, baking chocolate, cocoa powder, chocolate-covered snacks.

name: Grapes, raisins & currants
summary: Can cause sudden kidney injury in dogs; sensitivity varies a lot between individuals.
clinical_signs: vomiting; lethargy; reduced urination
common_sources: Fresh grapes, raisins, trail mix, baked goods, some snack bars.
dose_warning: No amount is known to be safe.

name: Onion, garlic, chives & leeks
summary: Damage red blood cells; cats are especially sensitive. Powdered and cooked forms count too.
clinical_signs: weakness; pale gums; red or brown urine; rapid breathing
common_sources: Cooked dishes, broths, baby food, onion/garlic powder, some supplements.

name: Macadamia nuts
summary: Cause weakness, tremors, and overheating in dogs; effects in cats are not reported.
clinical_signs: weakness in the back legs; tremors; vomiting; fever
common_sources: Mixed nuts, cookies, candies, baked goods.

name: Alcohol (ethanol)
summary: Found in drinks, raw dough, and some products. Even small amounts are dangerous to pets.
clinical_signs: stumbling; disorientation; vomiting; slow breathing
common_sources: Alcoholic drinks, raw bread dough, rum-soaked desserts, some sanitizers.

name: Caffeine (coffee, tea, energy drinks)
summary: A stimulant; grounds, tea bags, and pills are especially concentrated.
clinical_signs: restlessness; racing heart; tremors; vomiting
common_sources: Coffee, grounds, tea, energy drinks, caffeine pills, pre-workout powders.

name: Raw bread / yeast dough
summary: Rises and ferments in the stomach, producing gas and alcohol.
clinical_signs: bloated or painful belly; retching; weakness; disorientation
common_sources: Rising bread, pizza, or roll dough left within reach.

name: Salt & salty dough ornaments
summary: Large amounts of salt (table salt, salt-dough crafts, ice-melt) can dangerously raise blood sodium.
clinical_signs: vomiting; excessive thirst; tremors; stumbling
common_sources: Salt-dough ornaments, ice-melt, large amounts of salty food, sea water.

name: Moldy food & compost
summary: Mold can contain tremorgenic mycotoxins that quickly cause tremors and seizures.
clinical_signs: tremors; agitation; vomiting; high temperature
common_sources: Garbage, compost bins, spoiled dairy, moldy bread or nuts.

name: Fatty / greasy foods
summary: Rich, fatty scraps can trigger pancreatitis, especially in prone dogs.
clinical_signs: vomiting; diarrhea; painful belly; loss of appetite
common_sources: Bacon, fat trimmings, fried foods, gravy, holiday table scraps.

name: Green/raw potato & green tomato
summary: Green parts, sprouts, and stems contain solanine; cooked ripe flesh is generally fine.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; diarrhea; lethargy
common_sources: Sprouted or green potatoes, potato plants, unripe tomatoes and their plants.

name: Avocado
summary: The flesh causes mild stomach upset in dogs and cats; the large pit is a choking and obstruction risk.
clinical_signs: vomiting; diarrhea
common_sources: Guacamole, avocado flesh, pits, and the plant.

name: Lily (true & day lilies)
summary: For CATS, every part — even pollen or vase water — can cause fatal kidney failure; keep them out of the home entirely. In dogs, true lilies usually cause only mild stomach upset.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; hiding; reduced urination
common_sources: Cut-flower bouquets, Easter lilies, garden day lilies, the vase water.

name: Sago palm (cycad)
summary: All parts, especially the seeds, are highly toxic and can cause liver failure.
clinical_signs: vomiting; dark stool; jaundice; weakness
common_sources: Ornamental houseplants and landscaping, especially in warm climates.

name: Oleander
summary: Contains cardiac glycosides that affect heart rhythm; all parts are toxic.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; abnormal heart rate; collapse
common_sources: Outdoor landscaping shrubs, clippings, and bouquets.

name: Azalea / rhododendron
summary: Grayanotoxins affect the gut and heart; even a few leaves can cause signs.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; diarrhea; weakness
common_sources: Garden and landscaping shrubs, clippings.

name: Autumn crocus (Colchicum)
summary: Contains colchicine and can cause severe, sometimes delayed, multi-organ damage.
clinical_signs: drooling; bloody vomiting or diarrhea; weakness
common_sources: Fall-blooming garden bulbs.

name: Tulip & hyacinth (bulbs)
summary: The bulbs hold the most toxin; can cause heavy drooling and stomach upset.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; diarrhea
common_sources: Spring garden bulbs, potted bulbs, planting season.

name: Daffodil (Narcissus)
summary: Bulbs are the most toxic part; can cause vomiting and heart or breathing changes.
clinical_signs: vomiting; drooling; belly pain; abnormal heart rate
common_sources: Spring bulbs and cut flowers.

name: Dieffenbachia (dumb cane)
summary: Insoluble calcium oxalate crystals cause intense mouth irritation and swelling.
clinical_signs: pawing at the mouth; drooling; swelling of the mouth or tongue; vomiting
common_sources: Common leafy houseplant.

name: Philodendron & pothos
summary: Common houseplants with oxalate crystals that irritate the mouth and throat.
clinical_signs: drooling; pawing at the mouth; vomiting
common_sources: Trailing/hanging houseplants.

name: Peace lily (Spathiphyllum)
summary: Not a true lily — it irritates the mouth and throat rather than the kidneys, but still avoid it.
clinical_signs: drooling; oral pain; vomiting
common_sources: Flowering houseplant.

name: Cyclamen
summary: The roots and tubers are the most toxic part and can affect the heart.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; diarrhea; abnormal heart rhythm
common_sources: Flowering potted houseplant, popular in winter.

name: Kalanchoe
summary: A popular flowering houseplant containing heart-affecting toxins.
clinical_signs: vomiting; diarrhea; abnormal heart rate
common_sources: Flowering succulent houseplant.

name: Yew (Taxus)
summary: Contains taxines that affect the heart; all parts except the red flesh are toxic.
clinical_signs: trembling; difficulty breathing; sudden collapse
common_sources: Evergreen landscaping shrubs and clippings.

name: Foxglove (Digitalis)
summary: Contains cardiac glycosides; all parts affect the heart.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; abnormal or slow heart rate; weakness
common_sources: Garden flowers and bouquets.

name: Lily of the valley
summary: Despite the name it affects the heart, via cardiac glycosides.
clinical_signs: vomiting; abnormal heart rate; disorientation; collapse
common_sources: Shade garden ground cover and bouquets.

name: Castor bean / ricin
summary: The beans contain ricin, one of the most toxic plant compounds known.
clinical_signs: bloody diarrhea; vomiting; weakness; tremors
common_sources: Ornamental plants, some mulch, jewelry made from seeds.

name: Aloe vera
summary: The latex/gel can cause stomach upset in dogs and cats.
clinical_signs: vomiting; lethargy; diarrhea
common_sources: Houseplants and some topical gels.

name: Jade plant
summary: A common succulent that can cause stomach upset and incoordination; the exact toxin is unknown.
clinical_signs: vomiting; lethargy; incoordination
common_sources: Popular succulent houseplant.

name: Marijuana / THC (edibles & plants)
summary: THC affects the nervous system; edibles may also contain chocolate or xylitol, adding more risk.
clinical_signs: stumbling; dribbling urine; dazed or sleepy; low heart rate; startling at sounds
common_sources: Edibles, dried plant, concentrates, second-hand smoke.

name: Wild mushrooms
summary: Some wild or yard mushrooms cause liver failure or neurologic signs, and identification is unreliable — any ingestion is an emergency.
clinical_signs: vomiting; diarrhea; jaundice; tremors; seizures
common_sources: Lawns, woods, and damp shaded areas after rain.

name: Nicotine (cigarettes, vapes, gum, patches)
summary: Concentrated nicotine (vape liquid, gum, patches, butts) is rapidly toxic to pets.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; racing or abnormal heart rate; tremors; weakness
common_sources: Cigarettes and butts, vape liquid, nicotine gum and patches.

name: Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria)
summary: Toxic algae blooms in warm, stagnant water can cause rapid liver failure or neurologic collapse.
clinical_signs: vomiting; diarrhea; weakness; tremors; collapse
common_sources: Warm, still ponds and lakes with green/blue surface scum.

name: Antifreeze (ethylene glycol)
summary: Sweet-tasting and rapidly causes kidney failure; even a tiny amount is deadly, especially to cats. Time matters enormously.
clinical_signs: stumbling as if drunk; excessive thirst; vomiting; later, reduced urination
common_sources: Radiator coolant leaks/spills, garages, driveways.
dose_warning: Even a small lick can be fatal — do not wait.

name: Slug & snail bait (metaldehyde)
summary: Causes severe tremors and seizures soon after ingestion.
clinical_signs: tremors; twitching; seizures; high temperature
common_sources: Garden slug/snail pellets.

name: Bleach & concentrated cleaners
summary: Concentrated or strongly acidic/alkaline cleaners are caustic and can burn the mouth, throat, and airways.
clinical_signs: drooling; mouth pain; vomiting; coughing
common_sources: Household cleaning products, especially undiluted.

name: Laundry & dishwasher pods
summary: The concentrated detergent bursts under pressure and can cause vomiting and airway irritation.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; coughing or gagging; squinting if it contacts the eyes
common_sources: Single-use laundry and dishwasher detergent packets.

name: Zinc (pennies, hardware, zinc creams)
summary: Swallowed zinc objects and zinc-oxide creams can destroy red blood cells.
clinical_signs: vomiting; pale or yellow gums; red or brown urine; weakness
common_sources: Pennies minted after 1982, nuts/bolts, zinc-oxide skin creams.

name: Batteries (button / lithium)
summary: Cause caustic burns if chewed or swallowed; button/coin batteries are especially dangerous.
clinical_signs: drooling; mouth pain; vomiting; not eating
common_sources: Remotes, toys, key fobs, hearing aids, electronics.

name: Fertilizers & plant foods
summary: Most cause stomach upset; some contain iron, pesticides, or 'meal' additives that are more dangerous.
clinical_signs: drooling; vomiting; diarrhea
common_sources: Lawn and garden fertilizers, bone/blood meal amendments.

name: Anticoagulant rat / mouse bait
summary: Stops blood from clotting; signs can be delayed several days. Bring the product packaging to the vet if you can.
clinical_signs: weakness; pale gums; coughing; bruising; bleeding that won't stop
common_sources: Rodent bait stations in homes, garages, and sheds.

name: Bromethalin rat / mouse bait
summary: A non-anticoagulant bait that causes brain swelling; identifying the exact product matters, so keep the packaging.
clinical_signs: tremors; stumbling; weakness; seizures
common_sources: Rodent bait stations; the active ingredient varies by brand.

name: Ibuprofen & naproxen (human NSAIDs)
summary: Common human pain relievers; cause stomach ulcers and kidney injury. Cats are extremely sensitive.
clinical_signs: vomiting (sometimes bloody); not eating; lethargy; increased thirst
common_sources: Human medicine cabinets, dropped pills, purses.

name: Acetaminophen / paracetamol (Tylenol)
summary: Even one tablet can be fatal to a CAT by damaging red blood cells; dogs also risk liver damage.
clinical_signs: pale, muddy, or bluish gums; swelling of the face or paws; trouble breathing; vomiting
common_sources: Human pain/cold medicines, combination products.
dose_warning: There is no safe at-home amount for cats.

name: Aspirin (human)
summary: Human aspirin can cause stomach ulcers and bleeding and should only be used under veterinary direction.
clinical_signs: vomiting; dark stool; loss of appetite; weakness
common_sources: Human medicine cabinets; some combination products.

name: ADHD medications (amphetamine, methylphenidate)
summary: Even a small amount of these stimulants can be life-threatening.
clinical_signs: hyperactivity; racing heart; tremors; high temperature; seizures
common_sources: Prescription stimulant pills.

name: Antidepressants (SSRIs / SNRIs)
summary: Medications like fluoxetine and venlafaxine can cause serotonin-related toxicity.
clinical_signs: agitation or sedation; tremors; high heart rate; dilated pupils
common_sources: Prescription pills and pill organizers.

name: Sleep & anxiety medications (benzodiazepines, zolpidem)
summary: Can cause heavy sedation — or paradoxical agitation — and unsteadiness.
clinical_signs: sedation; stumbling; agitation; weakness
common_sources: Prescription sleep and anxiety medications.

name: Decongestants (pseudoephedrine)
summary: A potent stimulant found in many cold and allergy medicines.
clinical_signs: restlessness; racing heart; tremors; high blood pressure
common_sources: Cold, sinus, and allergy medicines.

name: Iron & prenatal vitamins
summary: Iron-containing supplements can injure the stomach and, in larger amounts, organs. Plain pet vitamins are usually low-risk.
clinical_signs: vomiting (sometimes bloody); diarrhea; lethargy
common_sources: Prenatal and iron supplements, some multivitamins.

name: Vitamin D (high-strength supplements & some baits)
summary: Excess vitamin D (from high-strength supplements or cholecalciferol bait) raises calcium and can cause kidney failure.
clinical_signs: increased thirst and urination; vomiting; weakness; not eating
common_sources: High-strength vitamin D supplements, psoriasis creams, some rodent bait.

name: Tea tree (melaleuca) oil
summary: Concentrated tea tree oil is toxic to dogs and cats even in small amounts, whether on the skin or swallowed; cats are most at risk.
clinical_signs: drooling; weakness; tremors; wobbliness; low temperature
common_sources: Pure essential oil, some 'natural' skin and flea products.

name: Pennyroyal oil
summary: An essential oil sometimes marketed for fleas that can cause liver failure.
clinical_signs: vomiting; lethargy; jaundice
common_sources: Herbal flea remedies and concentrated oils.

name: Wintergreen oil
summary: Contains salicylates (aspirin-like compounds) that are harmful to pets.
clinical_signs: vomiting; dark stool; weakness
common_sources: Pure essential oil, some muscle rubs and liniments.

name: Eucalyptus & citrus oils
summary: Diffused or applied essential oils can irritate or sicken pets; cats cannot process many oils and are most at risk.
clinical_signs: drooling; wobbliness; vomiting; skin or eye irritation
common_sources: Diffusers, cleaning products, 'natural' sprays, concentrated oils.
